incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, reports that scammers are using artificial intelligence to impersonate him and defraud vulnerable immigrants. The criminals have created hundreds of fake videos and social media profiles featuring AI-generated images of Leal promoting immigration services he never offers. In one video, the fake Leal advertises US residency assistance for $2,200 to undocumented immigrants without deportation orders. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, though suspicious activity first appeared in October. The situation has significantly worsened over the past three months.

To combat the fraud, Leal's office hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles across social media platforms, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. Scammers typically direct victims through social media videos to WhatsApp, where they send fraudulent contracts and request payment via Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the scams. He advises immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to be cautious of immediate payment requests.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake news article circulated online claiming that Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated article, which never actually occurred, exemplifies a rising wave of AI-generated investment scams. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research reveals that scammers increasingly use deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to create convincing but fraudulent investment schemes. The regulator took down 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of most commonly impersonated Australians, followed by politicians like Pauline Hanson and Jacqui Lambie. Finance professionals Alan Kohler and Tom Piotrowski are also frequently impersonated. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, positive reviews, and advertisements to lure victims. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing. Alan Kohler has called for heavy penalties against platforms hosting such content and the AI systems generating it.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A proposed class-action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco accuses Oura, the smart ring company valued at 11 billion dollars, of false advertising regarding its sleep tracking accuracy. The suit claims that Oura's rings, which cost 300 dollars and up, cannot accurately measure different sleep stages as advertised because their sensors and algorithms lack the capability to detect the physiological signals that hospital sleep labs use. The lawsuit alleges that Oura's marketing falsely claims 95 percent sleep staging accuracy and relies instead on artificial intelligence guesses that are no better than random chance, deceiving consumers about the product's actual capabilities.

Oura responded by defending its science and accuracy claims, stating that its rings estimate sleep stages using multiple physiological signals and have been validated in peer-reviewed studies. The company acknowledged that its product is not a medical device and should not replace clinical sleep studies. This marks the second lawsuit against Oura, following a previous class-action suit alleging the company collected personal information without consent. Experts note that consumer health trackers provide only estimates and should not be relied upon as definitive medical measurements, with more independent research needed to evaluate such devices.

incidents.title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations
incidents.summary:
Minnesota attorney Faisal S. Ahmed was suspended for submitting fake legal case citations generated by artificial intelligence in a court filing. Ahmed cited two nonexistent cases, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, in a 2025 memorandum filed in Hennepin County Court to support his client's position in a civil dispute. The opposing attorney discovered the fabricated citations and alerted the judge. Ahmed also included a false quotation from a real case and made additional citation errors in the brief.

Judge Lois Conroy ruled against Ahmed's client and ordered defendants to pay $233,563 in back rent. She fined Ahmed $5,000 and referred him to the Minnesota Lawyer's Professional Responsibility Board. Ahmed subsequently agreed to a 30-day suspension of his law license and to pay an additional $900 in costs. The judge emphasized that artificial intelligence tools should not replace proper legal analysis, noting that over 800 documented instances of AI-generated fake legal citations have been catalogued.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments and is abusing Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation. The researchers identified exposed infrastructure revealing Aurora's operations across multiple victim organizations. The ESXi ransomware variant uses ChaCha20 encryption and includes an ESXi mode that targets virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can read ransom demands. Aurora operators deployed a custom tool called esxi_finder.py to scan networks for ESXi hosts and vCenter servers by scanning ports 443 and 902.

Between April 8 and May 21, 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent across ten target organizations to perform various exploitation tasks including installing VPN clients, scanning internal networks with Nmap and NetExec, enumerating domain privileges, and attempting NTLM relay attacks. The operators imposed strict restrictions on the AI agent, forbidding DCSync attacks, account lockouts, and adding computer objects to domains. Researchers also identified a second Aurora cluster using different techniques, including SQL Server exploitation and S3 bucket exfiltration, affecting eight victim organizations across multiple countries.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
A major Pizza Hut franchisee filed a lawsuit in Texas claiming the chain's new AI-powered delivery system, called Dragontail, caused more than $100 million in damages. Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut locations across five northeastern states, alleges the system created cascading operational problems after it gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen workflows. According to the suit, drivers began waiting up to 15 minutes to batch multiple orders together rather than delivering pizzas immediately, causing delivery times to increase and customer satisfaction to plummet. Before the rollout in 2024, Chaac maintained over 90 percent on-time delivery and double-digit sales growth, but afterward the company experienced sharp declines, including a swing from positive 10.19 percent to negative 9.78 percent year-over-year sales growth in New York City.

Chaac argues Pizza Hut breached their franchise agreement by mandating the software's use while refusing adequate training and support as performance metrics worsened. The franchisee claims the system had obvious incompatibilities with their business model and that drivers could also see tip amounts and payment methods, making them selective about deliveries. Pizza Hut stated it was reviewing the lawsuit claims and would respond through appropriate legal channels. The case arrives as Pizza Hut faces broader struggles, with parent company Yum! Brands planning to close 250 US locations this year as the brand continues experiencing declining sales.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other staff members of NPR's "Fresh Air" program to defraud people. The fraudulent emails target authors, entertainers and public figures with personalized invitations to appear on the show, complete with details about their work and proposed interview topics. Eventually, victims are asked to pay fees, typically around $250, for supposed production costs. Jennifer Black, a history professor at Misericordia University, received such an email and initially felt flattered before recognizing red flags like the request for payment and the unusual involvement of Gross herself in logistics.

Experts attribute the sophistication of these scams to artificial intelligence technology, which enables criminals to personalize their impersonations convincingly. Similar scams have targeted other celebrities including comedians Nikki Glaser and Amy Poehler and journalist Katie Couric. WHYY, NPR and "Fresh Air" have stated they never charge guests for interviews and are working with law enforcement to investigate. Cybersecurity experts recommend verifying suspicious emails by contacting organizations directly and watching for red flags like payment requests or emails from non-official accounts.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
A fake think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. The institute, which has no legal entity, physical address, or named staff, presented pro-Israel arguments on controversial topics including alleged war crimes, genocide accusations, and starvation in Gaza. The content was formatted to appear academically rigorous with citations from legitimate sources like the UN and Amnesty International, but consistently framed information to minimize criticism of Israel by noting that no court has ruled on genocide claims and attributing casualty figures as coming from parties involved in the conflict.

The broader campaign, financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government and routed through European advertising firm Havas Media, aims to manipulate how AI systems respond to user queries. While Piro Inc, the American production company distributing the material, was paid $1 million, Clock Tower X received $15 million and other contractors received millions more. Israeli officials have expressed doubts about the campaign's effectiveness, with some calling it a waste of money as American public opinion has shifted sharply against Israel. Research analysts warn that the most concerning aspect is getting material into AI training data repositories, where false narratives could be regurgitated without citation or fact-checking.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, and Warner Music have filed separate lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno, accusing them of scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission. The labels claim both companies trained their models on massive amounts of protected music and are directly reproducing sections of famous songs. The record companies submitted extensive documentation showing they were able to recreate recognizable versions of well-known tracks by using specific prompts, demonstrating the AI systems had been trained on copyrighted material from artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, and many others.

The lawsuits, filed in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, argue that both companies have refused to disclose their training data and wrongfully claimed their use of copyrighted material constitutes fair use. The record labels provided a thumb drive containing AI-generated music samples that they say infringe on original recordings, including examples where prompts for specific decades and genres produced songs nearly identical to existing hits. The cases represent a significant legal challenge to generative AI services and their use of copyrighted content.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers apologized for using artificial intelligence that created fake legal cases, false quotes, and nonexistent legal holdings in court filings for a lawsuit in Los Angeles. The case involves Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, who sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire destroyed her home in Carson. While repairs were underway, water damage from a storm occurred, and Meni-Siliga said State Farm delayed approving repairs, leaving the work incomplete. She subsequently lost her home to foreclosure and declared bankruptcy.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted she used an AI tool called Irys that generated seven fake case citations across eight filings, incorrect case titles, and misquoted material. She mistakenly believed the tool was connected to her law firm's legal research subscription. Kenneth Katel, the lead lawyer on the case, accepted responsibility for the filings and said the firm updated its AI policy. The incident reflects a broader trend, with 41 percent of law firms now using generative AI. The case is scheduled for trial in October.

stories.Headline: Musk’s xAI loses court bid to block Minnesota’s AI ‘nudification’ ban - WTVB
stories.Summary:
Minnesota's law banning AI-generated fake nude images will remain in effect after a federal judge rejected Elon Musk's xAI company's request to block it. The law took effect on August 1 and prohibits website operators and software developers from allowing users to create artificial nude images of identifiable people. Judge Donovan Frank ruled that xAI failed to demonstrate it would suffer harm while pursuing its lawsuit, which claims the law violates free speech protections under the First Amendment.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison defended the measure as overwhelmingly bipartisan and nearly unanimously approved by state lawmakers. He stated that nudification apps have been used to generate child sexual abuse materials and harass people. xAI argues the law restricts constitutionally protected expression, while the state contends the measure is narrowly tailored to prevent nonconsensual sexual imagery. The judge acknowledged the constitutional issues are complex given the new technology involved and promised full consideration as the case proceeds.

stories.Headline: Nation’s Largest School District Bans AI In The Classroom Through 8th Grade - The Seattle Medium
stories.Summary:
New York City's public school system, the nation's largest, has implemented a one-year ban on generative artificial intelligence use for students in grades 2K through 8th grade. This moratorium affects approximately 600,000 students, representing nearly two-thirds of the district's total enrollment. Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced the policy, stating it aims to protect students' critical thinking abilities and preserve teacher-student relationships. The district will disable AI components in more than 38 previously approved educational programs that fail to meet new safety standards.

High school students will have limited access to specific AI tools and must complete AI critical thinking courses, while mainstream services like ChatGPT and Claude remain blocked across all grades. Teachers can use AI for lesson planning and operational tasks but not for grading or assessments. The policy includes exceptions for students with disabilities and English learners. A new Technology in Schools Coalition will evaluate the moratorium's effectiveness and provide recommendations for future years. The district also restricts individual screen time based on grade level, and New York state previously banned personal phones during the school day.

stories.Headline: Nevada lawmakers propose oversight for state, local agencies using AI - Kiowa County Press
stories.Summary:
# Summary

Nevada lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish oversight standards for how state and local government agencies use artificial intelligence technology. The bill draft request was approved in August by the interim Government Affairs Committee, with Democratic state Senator Dina Neal championing the proposal. The legislation would require transparency around AI systems and prevent bias in automated decision-making. Several Nevada agencies, including the Department of Employment, Training, and Rehabilitation and the Department of Motor Vehicles, have already implemented AI systems without statutory oversight. Concerns have been raised about cases where people were denied unemployment benefits and could not speak to a human during appeals, highlighting the need for human decision-making in critical processes.

The bill will be considered during the 2027 Legislative Session beginning February 1. Lawmakers anticipate significant pushback from state and local agencies when the proposal comes up for discussion. This effort reflects a broader national trend, as 38 states adopted AI-related policies in 2025. Nevada's push for AI regulation comes despite President Trump's efforts to limit state-level AI regulation through executive orders, though legal experts argue such orders may not prevent state action under constitutional protections for state authority.

stories.Headline: Nvidia buying artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face for $13 billion
stories.Summary:
Chipmaker Nvidia is acquiring Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence software platform, for approximately $13 billion. Hugging Face is used by over 18 million developers, researchers, and creators who share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets, and 1 million applications on the platform. More than 200,000 companies also use the service. Nvidia's CEO stated that Hugging Face will remain an open-source platform, allowing organizations to download and customize their own AI models rather than paying for proprietary services from competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic.

The acquisition represents Nvidia's strategic bet that businesses will increasingly favor open-source AI models. This deal comes amid growing concerns about AI security, following several incidents where AI systems hacked into other organizations during testing. The $12.93 billion purchase includes $1 billion for employee retention. Nvidia's stock rose nearly 2% following the announcement, while Hugging Face remains privately held.

stories.Headline: IIT Guwahati researchers unveil brain-inspired AI model for energy-efficient long-range data processing
stories.Summary:
Researchers at IIT Guwahati have developed a new artificial intelligence model inspired by how the brain works, designed to process long sequences of data while using much less energy than traditional AI systems. The team presented their findings at the International Conference on Machine Learning in Seoul in July. The model, called SHRFSSM, mimics how biological neurons communicate by only activating when important events occur, making it more efficient than conventional approaches.

The technology has potential applications in wearable health monitors, smart sensors, manufacturing systems, and weather forecasting. The researchers tested the model on seventeen different datasets and found it performed as well as existing advanced systems while consuming significantly less energy. The team plans to continue developing the technology for real-world use on devices with limited power and computing resources.

stories.Headline: Microsoft Tells Court Copilot Rarely Reproduces Books in AI Copyright MDL - Unite.AI
stories.Summary:
Microsoft filed legal arguments in September 2026 claiming that its Copilot AI system rarely reproduces copyrighted books. The company told a federal court in Manhattan that an analysis of 8.2 million Copilot conversations found only 24 responses containing at least 30 words matching passages from the authors' works, representing a rate of .00029 percent. Microsoft also argued that when experts deliberately fed book passages into the model hundreds of times to extract matches, fewer than 1 percent of attempts produced any 30-word matches. The case involves authors and publishers suing Microsoft and OpenAI over using copyrighted material to train their large language models.

Microsoft's main legal argument is that training AI on copyrighted books qualifies as fair use because the technology serves a transformative purpose. The company cited sales data showing no decline in book purchases since the AI systems launched and stated that most consumers would not buy AI-generated books even at lower prices. Microsoft also argued that data origin does not affect fair use analysis and that requiring licenses from millions of authors would stifle innovation. The case is pending before Judge Sidney Stein in New York federal court, with opposing briefs due by October 2026.

stories.Headline: LAUSD adopts moratorium on student AI use, another big move to limit classroom computer time - Los Angeles Times
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District has implemented a moratorium on student use of generative artificial intelligence on school devices for the current school year. District administrators enacted the policy independently to align with the school board's June decision to reduce student screen time, though some board members expressed surprise at not being formally notified. The moratorium prohibits chatbots and AI tutors for all students, though the district will continue using non-generative AI tools like adaptive learning systems and speech recognition software. Students can still use Google for searches but cannot access Google's interactive AI Mode on school devices.

The announcement comes as New York City also moved to restrict student AI use, banning generative AI in preschool through eighth grade while allowing limited use in high schools. Activist parents and education organizations praised Los Angeles's stricter approach as a historic step addressing concerns about technology reliance in schools. However, the district has not yet developed policies for student AI use on personal devices, and teachers remain able to use AI tools. Officials are working to determine long-term AI guidelines, as the moratorium currently applies only to the current school year.
